name: Common carp aquaculture at Jiahu, Henan
summary: Fish remains from Jiahu Period III (6200–5700 BCE) suggest that people at the Neolithic settlement were raising common carp in managed waters.
description: A 2019 study of fish bones from prehistoric East Asia argues, from the ages at which fish died and the species chosen, that common carp were being raised under management at the Early Neolithic site of Jiahu, Henan Province, by around 6000 BC. The claim rests on bone profiles, not on remains of ponds, and the study does not show that later Chinese carp farming descended from it.

impact.note: Raising fish instead of only catching them was a new capability, but it is shown for one Neolithic community and its region, and no later fish farming is shown to descend from it.

date.label: Jiahu Period III (6200–5700 BCE)
date.basis: Cultural period of the measured fish remains in Fig. 1b, the period assigned to the inferred management. The abstract summarizes it as by around 6000 BCE.

events.statement: From the distribution of estimated fish sizes and the composition of fish remains, Nakajima and colleagues infer common carp management at Jiahu in Period III (6200–5700 BCE).

evidence.supports: was present at the Early Neolithic Jiahu site, Henan Province, China, by around 6000 bc
The authors infer fish management in Jiahu Period III (6200–5700 BCE), based on estimated body-length clusters and the proportion of common carp.

events.caveats: The measurements support an inference of management. The evidence leaves the location and form of the managed waters unresolved.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The full paper assigns inferred management to Jiahu Period III (6200–5700 BCE). Seek Phase III landscape features or an independent assemblage that could distinguish water control from selective fishing.

The earliest transmitted version of the fish farming text attributed to Fan Li survives in the sixth-century CE Qimin yaoshu. The surviving text leaves its original date and continuity with Neolithic Jiahu uncertain.

evidence.supports: Traces the historical witnesses and explains why the text cannot be securely attributed to the historical Fan Li.

unresolved.note: Egyptian and Mesopotamian fish ponds were not checked, so whether Jiahu is the earliest aquaculture anywhere is open.

research.note: The study dates managed carp at Jiahu but does not compare it with other regions, so whether it was the earliest anywhere is not established.
